metadata.summary: Name the cause of steatosis, distinguish MASH activity from fibrosis, and classify alcohol exposure quantitatively.
metadata.application: Describe metabolic criteria, alcohol exposure, inflammatory phenotype, fibrosis evidence, and coexisting liver disease as separate parts of the assessment.
keyPoints: Steatosis plus at least one metabolic criterion supports MASLD.
MASH and fibrosis describe different features.
Fibrosis is central to liver-related prognosis.
Alcohol categories do not define a safe intake.

bodies.heading: Use current terms
bodies.body: Steatotic liver disease, SLD, includes several causes of hepatic fat accumulation. MASLD replaces the historical NAFLD name, and MASH replaces NASH. When interpreting an older trial, retain its actual inclusion criteria and alcohol limits; a new name does not expand the population studied or establish treatment eligibility.

bodies.heading: Establish the metabolic phenotype
bodies.body: In an adult with hepatic steatosis, MASLD requires at least one of five cardiometabolic criteria involving adiposity, glucose, blood pressure, triglycerides, or HDL cholesterol. Obesity and diabetes are not both mandatory. Evaluate alcohol exposure and other discernible causes before assigning the final SLD subtype; metabolic and other liver disease can coexist.

bodies.heading: Separate activity from stage
bodies.body: MASH describes steatosis with hepatocellular injury, including ballooning, and inflammation. It can occur with or without fibrosis. Fibrosis describes scar and is the main determinant of liver-related prognosis. Steatosis on imaging or an elevated ALT alone does not establish the full histologic MASH phenotype or a particular fibrosis stage.

bodies.heading: Classify alcohol explicitly
bodies.body: Record grams consumed, drinking pattern, frequency, duration, and changes over time. In the adult nomenclature, MetALD combines metabolic steatotic disease with approximately 140-350 g/week in females or 210-420 g/week in males, corresponding to 20-50 or 30-60 g/day. Higher intake favors primarily alcohol-associated liver disease. These are classification ranges, not safe-drinking limits; lower intake can still contribute to progression.

bodies.heading: Name what changes care
bodies.body: Record fibrosis evidence and its certainty rather than using fatty liver as the complete diagnosis. F3 denotes bridging fibrosis and F4 denotes cirrhosis; cirrhosis can be compensated before decompensation develops. Distinguish inflammation, scar, and complications. Liver-related risk rises with fibrosis, while cardiovascular and other competing risks remain relevant.

bodies.heading: Do not use normal enzymes as clearance
bodies.body: Aminotransferases reflect aspects of injury and may be normal in advanced disease. One normal ALT or the absence of symptoms cannot rule out clinically important fibrosis. Assess fibrosis risk with the appropriate pathway and reconcile any disagreement between laboratory results, imaging, and clinical findings.

check.question: Which feature most strongly informs liver-related prognosis in MASLD?
choices: Fibrosis stage, interpreted with the clinical findings.
One normal ALT value that permanently excludes progression.
Ultrasound steatosis alone, which establishes a fibrosis stage.
Body weight alone, regardless of other findings.
check.rationale: Fibrosis is the main determinant of liver-related outcomes. ALT, the presence of steatosis, and body weight do not independently establish the amount of scar or exclude advanced disease.

metadata.summary: Connect fatty-acid supply and lipid handling to hepatocyte stress, immune signaling, and stellate-cell scar formation without assuming uniform progression.
metadata.application: Explain why the liver phenotype reflects metabolic load, tissue responses, and modifying factors rather than the amount of stored triglyceride alone.
keyPoints: Adipose insulin resistance increases fatty-acid delivery.
Lipid storage and lipotoxic injury differ.
Immune and stellate-cell responses link injury to scar.
Progression varies between patients.

bodies.heading: Build the substrate load
bodies.body: Adipose insulin resistance impairs normal restraint of lipolysis, increasing free-fatty-acid delivery to the liver. Excess carbohydrate supply can promote hepatic de novo lipogenesis, the synthesis of new fatty acids. The resulting phenotype depends on delivery, utilization, oxidation, storage, and export, not on one pathway acting in isolation.

bodies.heading: Distinguish storage from injury
bodies.body: Triglyceride in lipid droplets represents steatosis but is not equivalent to inflammatory injury or fibrosis. Lipotoxic lipid species and disturbed lipid handling can contribute to hepatocyte stress. Mitochondrial dysfunction, endoplasmic-reticulum stress, and inflammatory signaling are linked pathways; the amount of visible fat alone cannot describe their activity.

bodies.heading: Connect injury to scar
bodies.body: Stressed or injured hepatocytes and resident immune-cell responses contribute to inflammatory signaling and stellate-cell activation. Activated hepatic stellate cells deposit extracellular matrix, linking chronic injury to scar formation. Steatosis, inflammation, and fibrosis are related features, but their presence and severity are not interchangeable.

bodies.heading: Recognize heterogeneity
bodies.body: Genetic variation, visceral adiposity, diabetes, dietary exposures, activity, alcohol, and environmental or social conditions influence disease course. Similar BMI or liver-fat measurements can therefore coexist with different injury and fibrosis risk. MASLD can occur in people without obesity; body size alone does not exclude a metabolic phenotype.

bodies.heading: Keep the model within its evidence
bodies.body: These mechanisms describe interacting contributors, not a fixed timetable through which every patient progresses. AASLD notes that oxidative-stress markers are consistently observed in NASH, while the precise causal role of oxidative stress in humans remains uncertain. Genetic associations do not justify routine gene-based risk stratification for every patient. Use clinical fibrosis assessment rather than inferring a stage from a mechanistic explanation.

check.question: Which cellular response most directly links chronic hepatocyte injury to hepatic scar formation?
choices: Activated hepatic stellate cells depositing extracellular matrix.
Triglyceride storage alone assigning an F4 stage.
A single glucose measurement creating a histologic stage.
Ultrasound brightness measuring stellate-cell activity directly.
check.rationale: Stellate-cell activation and extracellular-matrix deposition produce scar in the injury response. Stored lipid, glucose values, and ultrasound steatosis do not themselves establish a fibrosis stage.

metadata.summary: Measure the adult metabolic criteria, quantify exposures, and investigate plausible competing causes before attributing steatosis or abnormal liver tests to MASLD.
metadata.application: Build a positive metabolic assessment and a targeted search for additional disease, with clear follow-up for abnormal findings.
keyPoints: At least one metabolic criterion is needed with steatosis.
Risk criteria are not treatment targets.
Other causes can coexist.
Medication exposure requires clinical causal assessment.

bodies.heading: Inventory metabolic risk
bodies.body: Assess weight history, central adiposity, blood pressure, glucose status, lipids, sleep-apnea risk, kidney and cardiovascular disease, and family history. Diabetes and multiple metabolic abnormalities increase concern for progressive liver disease. Normal BMI does not exclude MASLD; document the measured metabolic criteria rather than assuming that appearance establishes or rules out disease. Selected endocrine conditions may coexist; hypothyroidism associations remain mixed, and steatosis alone does not justify routine hormone screening.

bodies.heading: Apply adiposity and glucose criteria
bodies.body: The adult adiposity criterion is BMI at least 25 kg/m², or at least 23 kg/m² for Asian populations, or waist circumference above 94 cm in males or 80 cm in females, with ethnicity-adjusted thresholds where appropriate. The glucose criterion includes fasting glucose at least 100 mg/dL, two-hour post-load glucose at least 140 mg/dL, HbA1c at least 5.7%, type 2 diabetes, or its treatment. These are alternatives within each criterion; all measurements need not be abnormal.

bodies.heading: Apply blood-pressure and lipid criteria
bodies.body: The remaining adult criteria are blood pressure at least 130/85 mmHg or specific antihypertensive treatment; triglycerides at least 150 mg/dL or lipid-lowering treatment; and HDL cholesterol at most 40 mg/dL in males or 50 mg/dL in females, or lipid-lowering treatment. Steatosis plus at least one of the five criteria supports the metabolic phenotype. These classification thresholds are not individual treatment targets and do not determine fibrosis stage.

bodies.heading: Quantify exposures
bodies.body: Take an alcohol history in grams as well as beverage amount, pattern, and duration. Reconcile prescribed drugs, nonprescription products, and supplements with start dates, dose changes, indications, and the laboratory timeline. AASLD identifies amiodarone, tamoxifen, methotrexate, corticosteroids, 5-fluorouracil, and irinotecan as potential contributors to steatosis or steatohepatitis. Valproate is another potential hepatotoxic exposure. These exposures can involve different injury mechanisms; a list alone does not establish causality.

bodies.heading: Evaluate plausible alternatives
bodies.body: Initial assessment includes history, examination, a hepatic panel, CBC with platelets, glucose and HbA1c, lipids, kidney assessment, and appropriate viral-hepatitis evaluation. Persistently abnormal liver chemistries or an atypical presentation can support additional autoimmune serologies, transferrin saturation, ceruloplasmin, or alpha-1 antitrypsin testing according to the clinical question. Use the phenotype and test results to refine the evaluation rather than ordering every rare-disease test indiscriminately.

bodies.heading: Recognize a nutritional or genetic clue
bodies.body: Steatosis in a patient with marked malnutrition, short bowel, or prior bypass surgery warrants consideration of nutrient deficiencies such as choline or carnitine. Young age with neuropsychiatric findings and low ceruloplasmin can raise concern for Wilson disease. Marked LDL elevation, low HDL, and unusually early fibrosis can suggest lysosomal acid lipase deficiency. These clues prompt directed testing; they do not establish the diagnosis by themselves.

bodies.heading: Assess medicines in context
bodies.body: A patient with steatosis and a potentially implicated medicine needs a causal assessment, not automatic attribution to MASLD or automatic withdrawal of every drug. Review the timing, biochemical pattern, alternative causes, therapeutic need, and appropriate safety information with the treating clinician. If drug-induced liver injury is suspected, the response depends on its severity and clinical context; do not derive a universal stopping threshold or a class-wide prohibition from a historical list.

bodies.heading: Avoid a diagnosis of exclusion only
bodies.body: MASLD uses positive steatosis and cardiometabolic criteria, but positive criteria do not close the differential diagnosis. Viral hepatitis, alcohol, medications, autoimmune disease, and selected genetic or nutritional conditions may add to the liver phenotype and change management. Record what is established, what remains uncertain, which results need follow-up, and whether findings warrant specialist assessment.

check.question: A patient has hepatic steatosis and elevated liver enzymes. What is the best initial approach?
choices: Define metabolic criteria and exposures, then evaluate plausible competing or coexisting causes.
Assume MASLD explains every abnormality without reviewing history or medicines.
Assign a fibrosis stage solely from the ALT concentration.
Delay evaluation until jaundice or other symptoms appear.
check.rationale: Positive metabolic criteria support MASLD, while the history, examination, laboratory pattern, and exposure timeline guide evaluation for additional liver injury. ALT alone cannot stage fibrosis, and symptom absence does not close the evaluation.

masld-001.question: Which combination supports the adult metabolic phenotype of MASLD?
choices: Hepatic steatosis plus at least one defined cardiometabolic criterion, with alcohol and other causes assessed.
Elevated ALT alone, without evidence of steatosis or a metabolic criterion.
Obesity alone, without evidence of hepatic steatosis.
Hepatic steatosis alone, regardless of metabolic criteria or other causes.
masld-001.rationale: MASLD requires steatosis with at least one of five cardiometabolic criteria. Alcohol exposure and other discernible causes help classify SLD and identify coexisting injury; ALT, obesity, or steatosis alone is insufficient.

masld-002.question: An older trial enrolled patients using NAFLD and NASH terminology. How should it be interpreted after the nomenclature change?
choices: Translate the terms while retaining the trial’s actual metabolic, alcohol, and fibrosis inclusion criteria.
Assume every person with any SLD subtype was included in the older trial.
Ignore the original alcohol exclusions because NAFLD is now called MASLD.
Treat the name change as proof that the intervention is approved for every fibrosis stage.
masld-002.rationale: Updated terminology does not change who was studied or establish treatment approval. The original eligibility criteria remain necessary when applying historical evidence.

masld-003.question: An adult with BMI 22 kg/m² has imaging-confirmed steatosis and type 2 diabetes, drinks no alcohol, and has no other identified cause. Which interpretation is appropriate?
choices: The metabolic phenotype can meet MASLD criteria despite the BMI.
MASLD is excluded because obesity is mandatory.
Diabetes alone proves cirrhosis regardless of other findings.
Steatosis automatically establishes histologic MASH.
masld-003.rationale: Type 2 diabetes satisfies the glucose criterion; obesity is not mandatory when steatosis and another defined metabolic criterion are present. Neither diabetes nor steatosis alone establishes cirrhosis or histologic MASH.

masld-004.question: Which conclusion exceeds what an ultrasound report of steatosis and one elevated ALT can establish?
choices: Calling the findings definitive histologic MASH with a specific fibrosis stage.
Confirming that the report describes hepatic fat accumulation.
Assessing metabolic criteria and alcohol exposure.
Planning appropriate fibrosis-risk assessment.
masld-004.rationale: Steatosis imaging and ALT do not show all histologic features of MASH or determine the amount of scar. Metabolic, exposure, and fibrosis assessment remain appropriate.

masld-005.question: Which feature most strongly informs liver-related prognosis in MASLD?
choices: Fibrosis stage.
One normal ALT value.
Ultrasound brightness alone.
Body weight alone.
masld-005.rationale: Fibrosis is the main determinant of liver-related outcomes. ALT, the presence of steatosis, and body weight do not independently establish fibrosis severity or eliminate liver-related risk.

masld-006.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes MASH activity from fibrosis?
choices: MASH includes hepatocellular injury and inflammation and may occur with or without fibrosis.
MASH always means F4 cirrhosis.
Fibrosis and steatosis are interchangeable terms.
An elevated ALT directly provides a histologic fibrosis stage.
masld-006.rationale: MASH describes steatohepatitis, including injury and inflammation. Scar is assessed separately; steatohepatitis need not be accompanied by fibrosis and does not automatically mean cirrhosis.

masld-007.question: A patient has an established F3 fibrosis assessment but ALT within the laboratory reference range. Which interpretation is appropriate?
choices: Normal ALT does not negate the fibrosis finding or eliminate the need for follow-up.
Normal ALT proves that F3 has resolved.
A single ALT value can replace every fibrosis assessment.
The absence of enzyme elevation makes advanced fibrosis impossible.
masld-007.rationale: Aminotransferases can be normal in advanced disease. An established fibrosis assessment must be interpreted with the clinical picture rather than canceled by one normal enzyme value.

masld-008.question: A record lists F4 cirrhosis with no previous decompensation. Which interpretation avoids a staging error?
choices: Cirrhosis can be compensated; F4 and decompensation describe different aspects of disease.
F4 proves that decompensation has already occurred in every patient.
Compensated status means that no cirrhosis is present.
Absence of symptoms converts F4 into a steatosis-only diagnosis.
masld-008.rationale: F4 denotes cirrhosis. Compensated cirrhosis can precede decompensation, so document stage and complications separately instead of treating symptom absence as proof that scar is absent.

masld-009.question: A female adult with hepatic steatosis and type 2 diabetes regularly consumes 210 g of alcohol per week. Which SLD classification range fits this exposure?
choices: MetALD, with metabolic and alcohol contributions assessed together.
Pure MASLD because any amount of alcohol is irrelevant when diabetes is present.
Primarily ALD because any alcohol intake exceeds the female MetALD range.
Cryptogenic SLD because no metabolic criterion is present.
masld-009.rationale: The female MetALD range is approximately 140-350 g/week. This patient has a metabolic criterion and an exposure inside that range. The category does not establish a safe intake or exclude other contributors.

masld-010.question: An alcohol history says only social drinking. What information best supports SLD classification?
choices: Quantified grams, beverage amounts, pattern, frequency, duration, and changes over time.
The phrase social drinking without a quantity or pattern.
Only the type of beverage, without amount or frequency.
A normal ALT used instead of the alcohol history.
masld-010.rationale: Alcohol classification requires quantitative exposure and its pattern and time course. A vague descriptor, beverage type alone, or an enzyme result cannot provide that history.

masld-011.question: A male adult with steatosis and a metabolic criterion regularly consumes 490 g of alcohol per week. Which interpretation follows the adult nomenclature?
choices: The exposure is above the male MetALD range and favors primarily alcohol-associated liver disease.
The exposure is below the male MetALD range.
Diabetes makes the alcohol amount irrelevant to classification.
MetALD applies only when no metabolic criterion exists.
masld-011.rationale: The male MetALD range is approximately 210-420 g/week. A value of 490 g/week is above its upper limit. Metabolic disease may still coexist and should remain part of the assessment.

masld-012.question: Which interpretation of the MASLD and MetALD alcohol ranges creates an error?
choices: Calling an intake below a classification boundary guaranteed safe for liver disease.
Recording alcohol exposure in grams and reassessing it over time.
Considering combined alcohol and metabolic contributions.
Evaluating other plausible liver disease alongside metabolic criteria.
masld-012.rationale: Classification ranges organize SLD terminology; they are not safe-drinking limits. Alcohol can contribute to progression below a category boundary, and individual susceptibility varies.

masld-013.question: How does adipose insulin resistance contribute to hepatic lipid exposure?
choices: It increases free-fatty-acid release through impaired restraint of adipose lipolysis.
It suppresses fasting fatty-acid release more strongly than normal insulin action.
It removes the contribution of hepatic de novo lipogenesis.
It lowers fatty-acid delivery regardless of dietary substrate and lipid disposal.
masld-013.rationale: Adipose insulin resistance increases lipolysis and fatty-acid delivery. Hepatic supply and disposal interact; the mechanism cannot itself establish a fibrosis stage.

masld-014.question: What does hepatic de novo lipogenesis mean?
choices: Synthesis of new fatty acids, which can increase with excess carbohydrate supply.
Direct measurement of fibrosis from ultrasound brightness.
Removal of all stored triglyceride by immune cells.
Formation of cirrhotic nodules whenever blood glucose rises once.
masld-014.rationale: De novo lipogenesis is fatty-acid synthesis. Excess substrate can promote this pathway, but it is distinct from fibrosis assessment, complete lipid clearance, or proof of cirrhosis.

masld-015.question: Two adults have the same BMI but different liver fibrosis assessments. Which explanation is supported?
choices: Visceral adiposity, metabolic factors, genetic variation, and exposures can differ despite similar BMI.
Identical BMI requires identical fibrosis in every patient.
BMI directly measures stellate-cell activation.
One normal glucose value proves that all metabolic pathways are identical.
masld-015.rationale: Body size does not capture all drivers of injury and progression. Fat distribution, diabetes, genetics, alcohol, and other exposures can alter disease course, and fibrosis still needs clinical assessment.

masld-016.question: Which interpretation of hepatic triglyceride storage is incorrect?
choices: Treating stored triglyceride alone as proof of inflammatory injury and a specific fibrosis stage.
Recognizing lipid droplets as part of steatosis.
Distinguishing lipotoxic signaling from the amount of stored fat.
Considering lipid utilization and disposal alongside delivery.
masld-016.rationale: Stored triglyceride and visible steatosis are not equivalent to MASH activity or scar. Lipid handling, hepatocyte injury, and tissue responses must be distinguished.

masld-017.question: Which cellular response most directly contributes to hepatic scar formation after chronic injury?
choices: Activated hepatic stellate cells depositing extracellular matrix.
Hepatocytes exporting triglyceride in VLDL without a fibrogenic response.
Adipocytes storing neutral triglyceride without a hepatic injury response.
Lipid droplets alone serving as the direct source of all extracellular matrix.
masld-017.rationale: Stellate-cell activation links chronic injury responses to extracellular-matrix deposition. Imaging steatosis, glucose, and lipid storage are not direct measurements or automatic causes of a particular scar stage.

masld-018.question: Which relationship correctly connects lipotoxic injury to fibrosis?
choices: Hepatocyte stress and immune signaling can contribute to stellate-cell activation and matrix deposition.
Steatosis and fibrosis are synonyms.
Every patient follows an identical timetable from fat accumulation to cirrhosis.
Hepatic lipid delivery has no relationship to inflammatory injury.
masld-018.rationale: Interacting hepatocyte and immune responses contribute to fibrogenesis. Fat accumulation and scar remain distinct, and modifying factors produce heterogeneous progression.

masld-019.question: A patient asks whether an oxidative-stress marker proves the cause and stage of their liver disease. Which response fits the AASLD evidence?
choices: Such markers are observed in NASH, but their precise causal role in humans remains uncertain and they do not assign fibrosis stage.
The marker proves oxidative stress is the sole cause of every case of MASH.
The marker directly establishes F4 without clinical assessment.
The marker guarantees that a treatment targeting it will reverse all fibrosis.
masld-019.rationale: AASLD describes consistent oxidative-stress findings but uncertainty about their precise human causal role. A mechanistic marker does not establish a scar stage or guarantee therapeutic benefit.

masld-020.question: Which statement overextends a genetic association in MASLD?
choices: Routine gene-based risk stratification is required for every patient solely because variants affect lipid handling.
Genetic variation can contribute to heterogeneous disease course.
Clinical metabolic and fibrosis assessment remain relevant.
Selected unusual phenotypes can warrant evaluation for rare genetic disease.
masld-020.rationale: AASLD does not recommend routine gene-based risk stratification in all patients. This differs from considering a specific rare disorder when clinical clues justify directed evaluation.

masld-021.question: A patient has hepatic steatosis and type 2 diabetes, but testing also supports chronic viral hepatitis. Which interpretation is appropriate?
choices: Metabolic and viral liver disease can coexist and both require evaluation.
The metabolic criterion excludes any viral cause of liver injury.
Steatosis proves that the viral finding is irrelevant.
ALT alone identifies which disease explains every abnormality.
masld-021.rationale: Positive metabolic criteria do not close the differential. Viral and metabolic disease can coexist and change management; steatosis or one enzyme result cannot dismiss the viral evidence.

masld-022.question: An adult has hepatic steatosis and HbA1c of 5.8% but no obesity. How does the adult metabolic criterion apply?
choices: HbA1c at least 5.7% meets the glucose criterion; steatosis and this criterion can support the metabolic phenotype.
Only obesity can provide a metabolic criterion.
HbA1c must be at least 9% for any metabolic criterion to apply.
HbA1c of 5.8% independently establishes cirrhosis.
masld-022.rationale: The glucose criterion includes HbA1c at least 5.7%; obesity and established diabetes are not both required. Alcohol and competing causes still need assessment, and the criterion does not assign a fibrosis stage.

masld-023.question: A young adult with steatosis has neuropsychiatric findings and low ceruloplasmin. What is the best next interpretation?
choices: Evaluate for Wilson disease with appropriate directed testing rather than assigning all findings to MASLD.
Diagnose MASLD as the sole cause without further evaluation.
Treat low ceruloplasmin as proof of an F4 fibrosis stage.
Exclude genetic disease because steatosis is present.
masld-023.rationale: This pattern raises suspicion for Wilson disease and supports directed evaluation. The clues are not a diagnosis or stage by themselves; steatosis does not exclude another liver disorder.

masld-024.question: A patient with short bowel and marked malnutrition develops steatosis. Which contributor deserves consideration?
choices: Nutrient deficiency, including choline or carnitine, assessed in the clinical context.
A guarantee of obesity-associated MASLD despite the nutritional history.
An exact fibrosis stage obtained from the presence of fat alone.
Exclusion of any nutritional contribution because the liver contains fat.
masld-024.rationale: AASLD lists nutrient deficiency in settings including short bowel, anorexia, and bypass surgery as a less common cause to consider. Steatosis does not establish metabolic obesity or fibrosis stage.

masld-025.question: AASLD lists amiodarone as a potential contributor to steatosis or steatohepatitis. What does that listing establish for an individual patient?
choices: A reason for clinical causal assessment using the exposure timeline and other causes.
Proof that amiodarone caused the patient’s steatosis regardless of timing.
Evidence that all listed drugs cause injury by an identical mechanism.
A requirement to stop amiodarone automatically whenever steatosis is reported.
masld-025.rationale: AASLD lists amiodarone among potential contributors. An association on a list does not establish causality in a particular patient; timing, pattern, other causes, and therapeutic context still matter.

masld-026.question: A patient taking tamoxifen is found to have steatosis. Which evaluation is most appropriate?
choices: Review timing, metabolic factors, laboratory pattern, other exposures, and the treatment indication with the clinician.
Assume the drug caused every abnormality solely because it appears on a list.
Assume MASLD excludes any medication contribution.
Stop every prescribed medicine without assessing therapeutic need or causality.
masld-026.rationale: Tamoxifen can contribute to steatosis or steatohepatitis, sometimes alongside metabolic risk. Clinical causal assessment should guide management rather than list-based attribution or indiscriminate withdrawal.

masld-027.question: A patient receiving corticosteroids develops worsening glucose control and steatosis. Which interpretation fits the AASLD evidence?
choices: Corticosteroids can exacerbate metabolic factors and contribute to steatosis; assess the full clinical and exposure context.
Corticosteroids invariably produce the same histologic fibrosis stage in every patient.
The metabolic changes rule out a medication contribution.
One elevated glucose result proves cirrhosis.
masld-027.rationale: AASLD includes corticosteroids among drugs with potential mechanistic links to steatosis, including worsening metabolic comorbidities. This does not establish individual causality or assign a fibrosis stage.

masld-028.question: Which response to a historical list of hepatotoxic medicines creates an avoidable error?
choices: Stopping every listed medicine automatically without evaluating suspected injury, causality, severity, or therapeutic need.
Reconciling prescription and supplement start dates and dose changes.
Considering coexisting metabolic and other liver disease.
Reviewing suspected drug-induced injury with the treating clinician.
masld-028.rationale: Potential hepatotoxicity warrants assessment in context. Lists do not justify indiscriminate withdrawal or a universal stopping threshold; suspected injury requires a severity-appropriate clinical response.
